narrative:
The 2020 Los Angeles Dodgers arrived in a shortened, pandemic-altered season with a singular mission: end a championship drought that had stretched more than three decades. Playing in empty stadiums and a bubble environment, they wasted little time establishing themselves as the class of baseball, going 43-17 in the 60-game sprint and outscoring opponents by a staggering 136 runs. With a deep rotation, a potent lineup anchored by Mookie Betts and Corey Seager, and a bullpen that was mostly reliable, this was a team built to go the distance.

The early going had its rough edges — a brutal late-July outing where Blake Treinen was torched for a key double that cost the Dodgers a game illustrated that even the best teams bleed sometimes. But August was where the Dodgers truly announced themselves, going 21-7 and overwhelming opponents with home run power. AJ Pollock delivered a stunning three-run blast against Colorado that changed a game, and contributions came from all corners of the roster. The month wasn't without turbulence — August 25th saw a devastating collapse against San Francisco as the bullpen imploded with back-to-back disasters — but the losses were exceptions in an otherwise dominant stretch.

September brought more of the same excellence, a 17-7 record cementing their status as the best team in baseball. Mookie Betts continued to announce himself as the signature acquisition of the Dodgers' dynasty project, and the lineup churned through opponents with relentless efficiency. There were bumps — Caleb Ferguson surrendered a brutal Kevin Pillar grand slam to Colorado, and Treinen gave up a late-game homer to Oakland — but the Dodgers kept winning, kept pitching, and kept setting the stage for October.

The postseason brought high drama and a moment of almost-heartbreak that threatened to define the entire run. The NLCS against Atlanta saw Will Smith deliver a massive three-run blast to swing a pivotal game, and Cody Bellinger added crucial power to help the Dodgers advance. Then came the World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays — a gritty, hard-fought series that nearly ended in stunning fashion when Brett Phillips stroked a walk-off single in Game 4 that scored two runs and silenced Dodger Stadium hopes in a moment of utter chaos. But Los Angeles regrouped, leaned on Corey Seager's World Series MVP performance, and finally claimed the Commissioner's Trophy in Game 6, ending 32 years of heartbreak and delivering Los Angeles its first championship since 1988.

chapters.title: Fast Start, First Blood
chapters.description: The Dodgers open the 60-game sprint with promise but suffer an early sting when Treinen is torched for a costly double.

chapters.title: August Dominance
chapters.description: The Dodgers go 21-7 in August, riding home run power and timely pitching to separate themselves from the pack, even as the bullpen shows cracks.

chapters.title: September Surge
chapters.description: A 17-7 September closes the regular season as Los Angeles rolls toward the playoffs, with Mookie Betts and the offense delivering moment after clutch moment.

chapters.title: Treinen's Trouble
chapters.description: Late September stumbles on the mound foreshadow bullpen concerns that will follow the Dodgers into October.

chapters.title: October Glory
chapters.description: The Dodgers fight through the NLCS and a wild, gut-wrenching World Series to finally claim the championship that had eluded them for 32 years.
